MOLECULAR PATHOLOGY REPORT
[redacted location] Medical Center
Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine

Patient: [redacted name]
MRN: [redacted ID]
DOB: [redacted date]
Specimen ID: [redacted ID]
Ordering Physician: Dr. [redacted name]
Date Collected: [redacted date]
Date Reported: [redacted date]

REFERRAL REASON
Microsatellite instability (MSI) testing requested for rectal adenocarcinoma. Patient meets Amsterdam criteria for familial cancer syndrome. Evaluation for possible Lynch Syndrome.

SPECIMEN INFORMATION
Tumor: Rectal adenocarcinoma biopsy, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue
Normal control: Peripheral blood
Tumor cellularity: 40% neoplastic cell nuclei

METHODOLOGY
Microsatellite instability analysis was performed using PCR amplification of five mononucleotide microsatellite markers (BAT-25, BAT-26, NR-21, NR-24, MONO-27) with the GeneScan MSI Analysis Kit. Fluorescently labeled PCR products were analyzed by capillary electrophoresis. Tumor DNA microsatellite patterns were compared to matched normal blood DNA to identify instability.

Technical Note: DNA was extracted from microdissected tumor tissue to ensure adequate neoplastic cellularity. Quality metrics met laboratory standards with DNA concentration >50 ng/μL and A260/A280 ratio of 1.8-2.0.

RESULTS
Microsatellite Instability Status: MSI-HIGH (MSI-H)

Marker Analysis:
BAT-25: UNSTABLE - Novel alleles detected in tumor
BAT-26: UNSTABLE - Novel alleles detected in tumor
NR-21: UNSTABLE - Novel alleles detected in tumor
NR-24: UNSTABLE - Novel alleles detected in tumor
MONO-27: UNSTABLE - Novel alleles detected in tumor

Summary: 5 of 5 markers demonstrate instability

INTERPRETATION
This tumor demonstrates high microsatellite instability (MSI-H) with instability detected in all five mononucleotide markers tested. MSI-H status indicates a defect in the DNA mismatch repair system, which may be due to germline mutations in mismatch repair genes (Lynch Syndrome) or somatic hypermethylation of the MLH1 promoter.

Given the patient's clinical history meeting Amsterdam criteria for familial cancer syndrome, these findings are highly suggestive of Lynch Syndrome. MSI-H tumors may have different prognosis and treatment implications compared to microsatellite stable tumors.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Referral to genetics counseling for evaluation of Lynch Syndrome
2. Consider immunohistochemistry for mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) to guide germline testing
3. If MLH1 loss is identified, consider MLH1 promoter hypermethylation testing
4. Family members may benefit from genetic counseling and cascade testing if Lynch Syndrome is confirmed

Reported by: [redacted name], MD, PhD
Board Certified in Molecular Genetic Pathology
